email.subject: Your temps and contractors haven't been paid. Nobody knows why.
paragraphs: The agency that supplies your temps and contract workers uses an outside payroll provider. This afternoon it went down.
This week's pay hasn't landed. The agency says “a delay.” The provider says “a technical issue.”
The contract sits with HR. IT has never seen it. Your organisation doesn't have a list of its contractors.
Some are on big contracts with a cushion. Some are on a few hours a week and need Friday's money.
email.question: What do you do first?
email.footnote: 2 minutes to your first decision. No login. A fictional scenario built on real patterns.

screens.title: Your temps and contractors haven't been paid.
chips: Some on a few hours a week

items: The agency says “a delay.” Its payroll provider says “a technical issue.”
Whether it's an outage or an attack

screens.title: Your first move.
screens.intro: Pick one or two. Your answers shape what happens next.

options.title: Build the list.
options.body: Find out who these workers are, and which departments are most exposed.

assumption.text: The list can be built from access records, purchase orders and managers' memories and can be completed in a few hours.

takeBack.label: Check whether you could build a list of every temp and contractor today, and note which sources you would use. Consider how you would keep this up to date.

options.title: Press the agency.
options.body: Use the contract to demand facts and a date.

assumption.text: The agency will prioritise your request and the contract gives you real leverage over their supplier.

takeBack.label: Find out what obligations rest on the agency and whether these are sufficient to protect your organisation.

options.title: Bridge the gap.
options.body: Arrange emergency payments to the most exposed workers.

assumption.text: Someone with the authority to approve an emergency payment can be found on a Saturday, and a lawful way to pay people outside the normal chain exists.

takeBack.label: Find out who could approve an emergency payment to contractors, and how long it would take.

options.title: Tell the workers now.
options.body: A short, honest message saying you don't yet know.

assumption.text: You know enough to say something that people will find reassuring and the gaps in your knowledge won't create greater anxiety. What you say will not be read as a promise to pay or an admission of fault.

takeBack.label: Draft the first message you would send to contractors, and note who must approve it.

options.title: Talk to the unions and worker reps early.

assumption.text: You can have a sensible conversation with workers’ representatives. Your proactive approach will be welcomed and they won't use the opportunity to increase tensions in the relationship.

takeBack.label: Find out who in your organisation talks to worker representatives, and meet them.
takeBack.from: Reveal 1, talk to the unions early

options.title: Protect the critical work.
options.body: Ask managers where their service depends on these workers, and notify them to develop a plan for absences.

assumption.text: You know which services these people keep running, and which of them are on your incident team.

takeBack.label: Identify the mission-critical work, and model the impact of reduced capacity on service levels.

screens.title: Who's holding the phone?
screens.intro: You chose to press the agency. The contract sits with HR. IT doesn't have a relationship or access to the contract. Choose one.

options.title: HR leads, IT supports.
options.body: The contract owner makes the call.

assumption.text: HR can run a supplier incident, has the standing to ask other teams for help, and will tell you early enough for IT to matter.

takeBack.label: Ask HR whether they are confident in running a supplier incident, and what they would want from IT.

options.title: HR asks for your help, and you step in alongside.
options.body: You form a small crisis management team together.

assumption.text: HR will ask, you have capacity, and a working relationship exists to ask through.

takeBack.label: Agree with HR now how they would ask you for help, and who would answer.
takeBack.from: Reveal 1, HR asks, you step in

options.title: You take the lead.
options.body: You take it from HR because you think they can't handle it.

assumption.text: HR will let go of it cleanly, the CEO will back you, and taking it is worth the risk to your relationship.

takeBack.label: Agree with the CEO and HR, in advance, when IT takes the lead and when it does not.

screens.footnote: No right answer. Each one leaves something behind.

screens.title: You're assuming…
screens.intro: Every move rests on something you haven't checked. Tap the flag on anything you'd check in your own organisation.

costBox.text: It depends on what happens next.

blocks.text: The agency calls back. Its payroll provider “cannot rule out” a security incident but says that there's no evidence personally identifiable information has been stolen. There isn't a timeframe for solving the problem.

blocks.message: Some of us won't come in Monday if we're not paid.
blocks.alert: Two of them are on your own incident team.

notes.text: Because you built the list, you can deal directly with contractors and make short-term arrangements.

options.title: Bridge the most exposed.
options.body: Arrange emergency payments for the workers who depend on this pay.

options.title: Brief the workers.
options.short: Tell the workers what you do and don't know
options.body: Say what you know and what you don't, before the group chat does it for you.

options.title: Escalate.
options.body: Ask the CEO / CFO for a decision on paying workers directly.

options.title: Find out what else is at risk.
options.short: Find out what else is at risk
options.body: Who else does this provider serve and how can you leverage those relationships?

options.title: Plan Monday without them.
options.body: Rota, priorities, what you'll stop doing.

screens.title: Before you see how it landed.
screens.intro: If this happened in your organisation, what would you do? Write it as you’d say it to your team. When the next incident hits, you can compare.
screens.privacy: No names or confidential detail. Write it as a pattern. Private to you: encrypted, and the author can’t read it. Timestamped, saved before the ledger.

screens.title: A quick forecast.
screens.intro: Three months from now, how does your organisation look compared with Friday? One tap. You'll compare it with what the Monday After shows.

options.title: Weaker, in ways I can't see yet
options.phrase: weaker, in ways you can't see yet.

screens.privacy: Only you and the author see your forecast.

screens.headline: Your assurance covered the agency. It never covered who pays the agency's workers.

summary.tally: So far: built up in {deposits}, drawn down in {drains}.

takeBack.label: Map who is paid through the same chain as your incident team.

variants.summary: You’ve spotted gaps in your supply chain management.
variants.detail: You have identified gaps in your understanding of supply chain risks. You've used the incident to build a clearer picture and make informed decisions next time.

variants.summary: Part of your own incident team is paid through the same chain.

detail.intro: How much you lean on contractors and suppliers, and how many layers deep.
detail.monday: Part of your own incident team turns out to be paid through the same chain as the workers who might walk.
detail.threeMonths: Nobody has mapped the organisation’s dependence on contractors.
detail.nextTime: The next failure exposes similar supply chain dependencies, gaps in your data and dependence on contractors.
detail.paper: Assurance covered the agency. It wasn't designed to interrogate the whole supply chain.

rows.summary: The agency was your only route to these workers. And they were dependent on at least one supplier. You haven't uncovered their other single points of failure.

detail.intro: Where one failure stops everything, and how many layers down it sits.
detail.monday: Your only route to these workers was one agency. It was dependent on one provider. One failed, so they both failed.
detail.threeMonths: The agency has promised a backup plan. Nobody has analysed how dependent your organisation is on the same supplier.
detail.nextTime: The next single point of failure is one you have not found yet, in a supplier nobody has asked you about.
detail.paper: Your supplier register lists the agency but does not map the supply chain.

takeBack.label: Pick one supplier and map its dependencies.

variants.summary: Three people carried the weekend, and now they're the only ones who know how it worked.

detail.intro: How much the people who carried the response have left, and who else can do what they did.
detail.monday: Three people carried the weekend. They did it well, so nobody asked who else could help. Other team members grumble about their lack of opportunity.
detail.threeMonths: The same three are called first for every incident. The work they put aside has not been picked up.
detail.nextTime: The next incident starts with the same three people, already tired. They're starting to depend on the overtime involved.
detail.paper: The incident plan names a team with all the usual suspects. There isn't a plan for what happens when they're burnt out.

variants.summary: The HR team is better placed to manage its suppliers.
variants.detail: The HR team has built capability to manage one of its key suppliers and now puts greater value on the IT assurance processes that your team requires.

variants.summary: Three people carried the weekend, and now they're the only ones who know how it worked.

detail.intro: How much the people who carried the response have left, and who else can do what they did.
detail.monday: Three people carried the weekend. They did it well, so nobody asked who else could help. Other team members grumble about their lack of opportunity.
detail.threeMonths: The same three are called first for every incident. The work they put aside has not been picked up.
detail.nextTime: The next incident starts with the same three people, already tired. They're starting to depend on the overtime involved.
detail.paper: The incident plan names a team with all the usual suspects. There isn't a plan for what happens when they're burnt out.

takeBack.label: Name the three people who carry every incident, and one person who could cover each.

variants.summary: IT is firmly in charge, but can it reduce risk?
variants.detail: The decision has expanded the scope of your IT function without increasing its budget or capacity. You're better placed to govern the response to the next problem but don't have the levers to reduce the likelihood that there will be a problem.

variants.summary: Finance, HR and IT worked together successfully and value IT’s governance processes more highly. How can you use that to increase compliance across the organisation?

detail.intro: How far people will rely on each other when it is not clear who is in charge.
detail.monday: Finance and HR paid people together for the first time, and each saw the other work under pressure.
detail.threeMonths: People know who to ring in the other team, and they have started ringing before it is urgent.
detail.nextTime: The next incident starts with relationships that already work. That only holds while the same people are in post.
detail.paper: The escalation route exists in a document. Whether anyone uses it depends on whether they have worked with the person at the other end.

takeBack.label: Book thirty minutes with your counterpart in Finance or HR before you need them.

variants.summary: You have a list of these workers that nobody had on Friday.

detail.intro: How much of the organisation you can see, and how quickly.
detail.monday: You have a list of these workers that nobody had on Friday.
detail.threeMonths: The list is already out of date unless someone owns it. Contractors have started and left since.
detail.nextTime: You start from a list, not a guess, if you keep it.
detail.paper: The contract register is complete. It lists the agency. It does not list the people the agency provides.

summary.todo: Visibility, Drain version (no list was built): one-line summary

takeBack.label: Find out whether one list of contractors exists, and who owns it.

variants.summary: You and HR settled who decides before the CEO had to ask.

detail.intro: Who is allowed to make which call, and whether everyone knows it.
detail.monday: The CEO asked who was leading and got one answer.
detail.threeMonths: The agreement was spoken, not written. People remember it differently, and the next contract will be signed without it.
detail.nextTime: The same question is answered in minutes, if the answer is written down.
detail.paper: The delegation scheme says who can sign off payments. But there wasn't clear governance for agreeing to step outside the process.

variants.summary: The CEO asked who was leading and heard two answers.

detail.todo: Decision rights, Drain version: detail page

takeBack.label: Write down who decides whether to pay workers outside the usual chain, and check they know it.

variants.summary: You decided what stopped first, so the rest of the work slowed on purpose.
variants.detail: You made a proactive decision to communicate that some work has slowed. Colleagues understand why and your teams are working under less pressure as a result.

variants.summary: Planned work stopped while you looked after this, and nobody counted what.

detail.intro: What the rest of the organisation did not get done because of the response.
detail.monday: Three people left planned work to cover the weekend. They are compensated but tired. What's the impact on their planned work?
detail.threeMonths: Two pieces of work have slipped. The reasons are not on any report.
detail.nextTime: The same work stops first again, because nobody agreed in advance what should.
detail.paper: The portfolio report is green for now. The impact of this weekend won't be visible immediately.

takeBack.label: List the work you would stop first in an incident, and tell the people it affects.

screens.footnote: Tap a row for three months on and next time. Flag what you’d take back.

screens.title: Take one thing back.
screens.intro: You flagged {count}. Pick the one you’ll actually do. One is enough.
screens.none: You didn’t flag anything this time. You can go back to the ledger and flag something, or close the file.
screens.followUp: Ask me in 30 days whether I did it. One email, and you can stop it any time.
screens.followUpPromise: I’ll ask you in 30 days whether you did.

middle.text: You now know who these people are.
You still don't have one list of these people.

1.did: You kept the most exposed people paid.
1.still: You still don't know who owns the supplier's supplier.

2.did: You said what you knew and what you didn't, before the group chat did.
2.still: You still can't say when anyone will be paid, or who owns the supplier's supplier.

3.did: You made it the CEO's decision, so it had an owner by Saturday.
3.still: You still haven't asked who should have owned the supplier's supplier before it mattered.

4.did: You know what else this provider touches.
4.still: You still haven't decided who watches it.

5.still: You still don't know who will be paid, or who owns the supplier's supplier.

mirror.fallback: You still don't know who owns the supplier's supplier.

screens.tagline: Lucky, or designed? Only one of those repeats.

recorder.text: Want a copy of what you wrote? We’ll email it to you. Nobody else can read it.
recorder.previewNote: In the finished version, this emails you a copy.

share.text: Send this to the person you'd most like to answer it differently.

team.text: Some of these questions are hard to settle alone. If you'd like to run this with your team, reply to this email and I'll show you how.

t1.title: Are you owning this?

intro.text: You stepped in alongside HR. The CEO has asked who is leading.
You agreed HR would lead. The CEO has asked who they should call.
You took it from HR. The CEO has asked who is leading, and so has HR.

options.title: Front it
options.body: You are the visible lead, to the CEO and to the workers.

reveal.assuming: You can carry the workers' trust and the CEO's confidence at once, and HR will not read it as a takeover.
reveal.gain: One clear voice. The CEO and the workers know who to call.
reveal.cost: HR's ownership weakens, and your name is on it if it goes wrong.

options.title: Back HR, visibly
options.body: You tell the CEO you are supporting the Chief People Officer.

reveal.assuming: HR can hold the room with the CEO and the workers, and you will hear in time if it slips.
reveal.gain: The owner of the relationship stays accountable, and your capacity is kept for the rest of IT.
reveal.cost: Your influence rests on someone else’s performance, and you may hear late.

options.title: Stay in the background
options.body: You help quietly and step forward only if asked.

reveal.assuming: You will be asked in time, and HR will tell you when it starts to slip.
reveal.gain: Your capacity stays free for the rest of IT, and HR keeps ownership of its own relationship.
reveal.cost: You hear late, and the delay is invisible until it is not.

t1.closing: All three can be reasonable. The question is who the CEO believes owns it.

t2.title: Who should have checked?
t2.intro: The agency passed assurance when you bought it. Nobody looked at who pays its workers.

options.title: IT
options.body: Knows the technology

reveal.assuming: IT knows what to look for in a payroll provider, and has the standing to ask for it.
reveal.gain: The check is technically sound, and it covers systems IT already protects.
reveal.cost: IT has to know the contract exists first. Here it never saw it, so the check never starts.

options.title: HR
options.body: Owns the relationship

reveal.assuming: HR has, or can buy in, the skill to judge a payroll provider's resilience.
reveal.gain: The owner of the relationship stays accountable.
reveal.cost: The check is shallow, which risks being paper again.

options.title: The agency
options.body: It's their supply chain

reveal.assuming: The agency is checking its own supplier, and will tell you honestly if it is not.
reveal.gain: The responsibility sits with the party closest to the supplier, and asking costs you nothing.
reveal.cost: You are relying on a statement, not evidence, from someone who loses the contract if the answer is bad.

options.title: Shared, by design
options.body: Agreed in advance, revisited as the supplier's role changes

reveal.assuming: Someone agreed in advance who checks what, and keeps that agreement alive as the supplier's role changes.
reveal.gain: Nothing falls between IT and HR, and the check is revisited when the supplier changes.
reveal.cost: It takes effort before anything has gone wrong, which is hard to justify, and agreements like this drift if nobody owns them.

t2.closing: All four can be reasonable. The question is whether anyone decided this agency was critical.
t2.disclaimer: A question about what a sensible owner would check, not what the law requires.

takeBack.label: Ask who should have checked the agency’s payroll provider.
takeBack.commit: Ask who should have checked the agency’s payroll provider, and write down the answer.

t3.title: The clock.

situation.text: The agency’s payroll provider “cannot rule out” a security incident. Pay data is personal data. What do you do about the clock?

options.title: Wait for confirmation
options.body: Nothing to act on until someone says it is an incident.

reveal.assuming: Nothing starts until someone confirms an incident, and nobody will later ask what you knew on Saturday.
reveal.gain: You do not raise an alarm over a maybe.
reveal.cost: If the clock runs from when you became aware, time has already passed, and you have no record of what you knew.

options.title: Note when you were told
options.body: Start a timestamped log of what you knew and when.

reveal.assuming: The record you start now will matter later, and someone else is deciding who reports.
reveal.gain: You can show what you knew and when.
reveal.cost: A log is not a decision. Someone still has to own the call.

options.title: Ask your data protection lead
options.body: Are you a controller or a processor here, and who tells the regulator?

reveal.assuming: You have a data protection lead, they can be reached on a Saturday, and they can say what your role is.
reveal.gain: You get a view early on whether you are a controller or a processor here, and who has to tell whom.
reveal.cost: If nobody can be reached, hours pass. And the honest answer may be "it depends".

options.title: Ask the agency in writing
options.body: Has it told its customers, and has its provider told it?

reveal.assuming: The agency knows what its provider has told it, and will answer in writing.
reveal.gain: You have a dated record of what you asked and what you were told.
reveal.cost: A written question can slow things down and make the agency defensive. It may not have the answer either.

t3.closing: The clock may start when you become aware, not when someone confirms.
t3.disclaimer: Questions to check with your data protection lead or counsel. Not legal advice.

chip.title: A neighbour will pay its contractors directly

t4.title: You're not the only customer.

situation.text: A neighbouring organisation that uses the same agency announces it will pay its contractors directly. Your workers have seen it.

t4.prompt: What do you do? Pick one.

options.title: Call the other customers and agree a common line
Wait and let them move first
Hold your line and explain why
Take it to a shared forum or the agency

t4.disclaimer: Coordinating with other customers may have limits depending on sector and country. Check before you act.
